title: Weight-Space Learning for Certifiable Few-shot Transfer Learning
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Prior meta-learning finds one good initialization and optimizes continuously; ours learns a solution manifold and discretely selects among sampled candidates.
layout: 2 rows by 2 columns, meta-train to meta-test, colored row backgrounds
description: The figure has two horizontal bands. The top band has a light blue background and is labelled MAML. It shows two 3D loss-surface plots, Meta-Train and Meta-Test, each with axes θ1, θ2 and Loss. In Meta-Train, a star marks the shared initialization θ⁰, with red, green and blue arrows pointing to three task optima. In Meta-Test, an orange path with steps 1 to 4 runs from θ⁰ down the surface to θ*. The bottom band has a light purple background and is labelled STEEL (Ours). On the left, a 3D torus manifold in θ1, θ2, θ3 space is surrounded by orange adapter points. A purple arrow leads to a purple box reading '1. Diffusion Model'. On the right, a second torus holds sampled points colored by loss, with a colorbar from red to green. Steps '2. sample' and '3. eval' lead to a starred θ* in a green label. The colored bands draw the eye first.
caption: Contrasting meta-learning paradigms. Top row (MAML): Traditional gradient-based meta-learning. During meta-training, MAML learns an initialization point $\theta^0$ positioned close to all task-specific optima. At meta-test, a few gradient descent steps adapt $\theta^0$ to the new task's optimum $\theta^*$. $\theta^0$ is the transferred meta-knowledge. \textit{Bottom row (\ourShort{}, Ours):} Manifold-based meta-learning. During meta-training, we collect adapters $\{\theta_i\}$ from upstream tasks and fit a diffusion model to capture their distribution---the task solution manifold. At meta-test, we sample candidates from the learned manifold and select $\theta^*$ by evaluating support set loss $r(\theta)$, replacing continuous optimization with discrete selection over a finite hypothesis space. The diffusion model is the transferred meta-knowledge.
abstract: In contemporary deep learning, a prevalent and effective workflow for solving low-data problems is adapting powerful pre-trained foundation models (FMs) to new tasks via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). However, while empirically effective, the resulting solutions lack generalisation guarantees to certify their accuracy - which may be required for ethical or legal reasons prior to deployment in high-importance applications. In this paper we develop a novel transfer learning approach that is designed to facilitate non-vacuous learning theoretic generalisation guarantees for downstream tasks, even in the low-shot regime. Specifically, we first use upstream tasks to train a distribution over PEFT parameters. We then learn the downstream task by a sample-and-evaluate procedure -- sampling plausible PEFTs from the trained diffusion model and selecting the one with the highest likelihood on the downstream data. Crucially, this confines our model hypothesis to a finite set of PEFT samples. In contrast to the typical continuous hypothesis spaces of neural network weights, this facilitates tighter risk certificates. We instantiate our bound and show non-trivial generalization guarantees compared to existing learning approaches which lead to vacuous bounds in the low-shot regime.
